Illustrative Contradictory Claims

Internal-to-patient factors Species The claims are based on different species, while differences in disease manifestation, biological mechanisms, and pharmacokinetics across species limit the direct comparability of drug effects.
Study 1 (PMID 26095960) Context: Sixty dogs scheduled for an ovariohysterectomy...
Claim: Maropitant... did not eliminate retching and vomiting.
Study 2 (PMID 27538868) Context: Eighty-three healthy female cats were randomized to...
Claim: Maropitant might be useful... to prevent emesis...
Contradiction explanation: The studies differ in the biological system (dogs vs. cats) in which the drug is tested.
Continued on next page Population The claims target different human subpopulations (age, sex, genetics, comorbidities, ethnicity, or risk profiles).
Study 1 (PMID 26775631) Context: ... at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center...
Claim: Rectal indomethacin did not prevent post-ERCP pancreatitis.
Study 2 (PMID 37982566) Context: ... in the First Affiliated Hospital of Dalian Medical University...
Claim: Rectal indomethacin is an effective and safe method to prevent pancreatitis for patients undergoing ERCP.
Contradiction explanation: The studies were conducted in different patient populations (United States vs.
China).
External-to-patient factors Dosage and exposure duration Different doses or exposure durations may produce different biological effects.
Study 1 (PMID 26850803) Context: ...
Experimental group inhaled lavender essence 5% for 10min, three times a week ...
Claim: Result does not support that lavender essential oil is effective on fatigue in haemodialysis patients.
Study 2 (PMID 39775962) Context: ...
Lavender essential oil was applied to the experimental group for 20min prior to going to bed... for 5 consecutive days...
Claim: aromatherapy with lavender essential oil significantly alleviated fatigue in patients with hematological malignancies undergoing chemotherapy.
Contradiction explanation: The two studies evaluate at different duration of lavender essential oil (10min vs. 20min).
Route or mode of administration Different delivery routes or timing may change tissue targeting or absorption.
Study 1 (PMID 27488327) Context: ... patients ... receive 300,000 IU intramuscular Vitamin D...
Claim: Vitamin D supplementation may have a beneficial role in ulcerative colitis patients.
Study 2 (PMID 30601999) Context: ... oral vitamin D supplementation ...
Claim: Vitamin D supplementation ... may worsen the symptoms of ulcerative colitis.

Contradiction explanation: The studies investigate different drug administrations (intramuscular vs. oral) Evolving scientific evidence Contradictions reflect different stages of scientific understanding, where early hypotheses are later revised by new work.
Study 1 (PMID 33175088) Claim: ...in patients with acute heart failure...
The reduction of the incidence of a composite of cardiovascular death or first rehospitalization for cardiovascular diseases by eplerenone is inconclusive because of inadequate power.
Study 2 (PMID 37370197) Claim: ... patients with heart failure...
Eplerenone provides statistically significant and clinically meaningful benefits shortly after treatment initiation in most patients...

Contradiction explanation: The first study reports the inconclusive results due to the inadequate statistical power, while the second study represent the larger and more definitive investigation confirming the significant clinical benefit of the drug, illustrating the progression from early-stage to established evidence.
Known controversy Claims explicitly acknowledge uncertainty, debate, or conditional validity, indicating an ongoing scientific controversy rather than a genuine conclusion.
Study 1 (PMID 28540436) Claim: ...melatonin was as effective as midazolam in reducing children's anxiety in both preoperative room and at induction of anaesthesia.
Study 2 (PMID 37953202) Claim: Melatonin was less effective than midazolam at reducing preoperative anxiety in children, although the early termination of the trial increases the likelihood of bias.
Contradiction explanation: Study 2 acknowledges that early trial termination may have limited the reliability of its findings.

Continued on next page Contextual Factor Description Illustrative Contradictory Claims Combined drug effect Contradictions can arise when a drug's reported effect depends on its combination with other medications, where drug-drug interactions or synergistic effects produce outcomes that differ across studies.
Study 1 (PMID 26903532) Context: ... early breast cancer with adjuvant anthracycline...
Claim: concomitant treatment with candesartan provides protection against early decline in global left ventricular function.
Study 2 (PMID 27348762) Context: during or shortly after trastuzumab treatment in early breast cancer...
Claim: ...
The findings do not support the hypothesis that concomitant use of candesartan protects against a decrease in left ventricular ejection fraction.
Contradiction explanation: Candesartan is evaluated with different co-treatment in two studies (anthracycline in the first study vs. trastuzumab in the second study).
The combined drugs have different mechanisms of cardiotoxicity that may affect the Candesartan's treatment outcome in different ways.

Study design Contradictions may arise from differences in trial methodology, such as parallel vs. crossover design, superiority vs. non-inferiority frameworks, blinding status, comparator type (placebo vs. active control), or randomization procedures.
Study 1 (PMID 28077507) Context: ... patients were categorized as having paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent AF (atrial fibrillation) patterns at randomization...
Claim: The efficacy and safety profile of edoxaban as compared with warfarin was consistent across the 3 patterns of AF.
Study 2 (PMID 34962979) Context: ...
Of 21105 patients with AF randomized to warfarin, edoxaban 60/30mg, or edoxaban 30/15mg...
Claim: edoxaban 30/15mg is inferior (vs. warfarin) for stroke prevention in AF patients with PAD.
Contradiction explanation: Study 1 evaluates edoxaban across all AF subtypes broadly, while Study 2 focuses specifically on AF patients with a co-morbidity, peripheral artery disease.
The different patient stratification strategies may result in different study outcomes.
Outcome measures Contradictions may arise when studies assess different outcomes or evaluate the same outcome at different time points.
Study 1 (PMID 26852138) Context: ... assessed emotion processing during the presentation of pleasant, neutral and unpleasant pictures...
Claim: ADHD patients show a reduced reactivity towards pleasant stimuli.
Methylphenidate (MPH) did not normalize this dysfunction.
Study 2 (PMID 27734305) Context: ...
Resting state functional connectivity (RSFC) analysis revealed significantly reduced connectivity under MPH compared to placebo...
Claim: MPH is 'normalising' a higher RSFC in young people with ADHD.
Contradiction explanation: The first study assesses behavioral emotion processing during stimulus presentation, while the second study evaluates resting-state functional connectivity.
These outcomes capture different aspects of ADHD, one reflecting behavioral responses and the other reflecting brain-level connectivity.
The differences in outcome definitions may lead to contradictory evidence.
One claim lacks a clear specification of species, population, dosage and exposure duration, or route of administration, resulting in uncertainty about the basis of comparison.
Study 1 (PMID 26822749) Context: ... maintenance dose 4 mg/kg per day ...
Claim: support the concept of neuroprotection with phenytoin in patients with acute optic neuritis at concentrations at which ...
Study 2 (PMID 32212009) Context: (no dosage information mentioned) Claim: Phenytoin is not probably safe and effective as neuroprotection after acute optic neuritis.
Contradiction explanation: The lack of dosage information in the second study abstract leading to ambiguity in interpretation of the second claim, prevents direct comparison between the two claims.
Building on this taxonomy, we leverage LLMs to identify the study-level factor differences that explain the contradictory findings of the claims.
Because a contradiction may come from several study differences at once, we treat explanation as a multi-label task.

Specifically, we design the prompt to instruct LLMs to: (1) analyze the full abstract context of each claim; and (2) assign one or more study-level factors that explain the discrepancy between the claims.
The output is structured as a set of study-level factor labels.
The detailed prompt is presented in Appendix B.3.

To establish ground truth for evaluating DrugCon's contradiction detection and explanation outputs, we apply DrugCon to a large RCT collection, annotate its predictions, and then exhaustively review the remaining claim pairs.
The resulting annotated dataset is DrugCon-Bench.
We collect all RCT abstracts published from 2016 to 2025 in the PubMed Central Open Access subset, identified using Cochrane's sensitivity-and precision-maximizing RCT query (Glanville et al.
We apply DrugCon with GPT-4.1-nano as the LLM backbone.
We choose GPT-4.1-nano for its low inference cost at the scale of this study and its high recall with the counterfactual prompt (Section 3.4).
High recall is preferred, since false positives can be removed by annotators.
Over the full corpus, claim pairing yields 609,877 candidate claim pairs, of which DrugCon predicts 615 as contradictory.
These predicted pairs involve 819 unique abstracts, which form the annotation scope of DrugCon-Bench.
To capture contradictions missed by GPT-4.1-nano, we exhaustively review all remaining claim pairs within these abstracts.
Four annotators participated: a biomedical informatics expert (HK) and three PhD students trained in biomedical NLP (ML, JM, and SL).
For each DrugCon-predicted pair, annotators were shown the two claims side by side with their full abstracts, the predicted contradiction label, and the predicted study-level factors (Figure 3).
text.formatted: For each DrugCon-predicted pair, annotators were shown the two claims side by side with their full abstracts, the predicted contradiction label, and the predicted study-level factors (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>).

text.text: They made two decisions: (a) whether the pair is an apparent contradiction, and (b) which study-level factors from the taxonomy (Section 2.4) explain it.

Detailed guidelines are provided in Appendix A. To calibrate annotators and measure inter-annotator agreement, all four annotators labeled a shared subset of 50 pairs over three stages, meeting after each stage to reconcile disagreements and refine the guidelines.
We stopped after the third stage because agreement had reached a satisfactory level (Section 3.1).
Agreement was measured with Gwet's AC1 (Gwet 2008), which is robust to the skewed label distributions.
text.formatted: Agreement was measured with Gwet's AC1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Gwet 2008)</ref>, which is robust to the skewed label distributions.

text.text: The remaining pairs were divided equally among annotators.
Exhaustive review.
To capture contradictions that DrugCon missed, we review every remaining claim pair about the same drug-disease association within the 819 abstracts.
One annotator (ML) identified 53 additional contradictory pairs, 48 of which were confirmed by a second annotator (HK).

We do not attempt exhaustive annotation over all 224,756 abstracts, since the number of claim pairs grows quadratically with the number of abstracts; even after claim pairing, the full corpus yields 609,877 candidate pairs.

Because all contradictions within the 819 abstracts are annotated, DrugCon-Bench supports closed-world evaluation, unlike prior datasets that annotate only a subset of contradictions (Alamri and Stevenson 2016).
text.formatted: Because all contradictions within the 819 abstracts are annotated, DrugCon-Bench supports closed-world evaluation, unlike prior datasets that annotate only a subset of contradictions <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alamri and Stevenson 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Corpus statistics are reported in Section 3.1.
We evaluate on two datasets.
DrugCon-Bench (Section 2.5) is our primary benchmark.
To assess generalization, we also use ManConCorpus (Alamri and Stevenson 2016), a manually curated benchmark of contradictory claims from cardiovascular RCT abstracts.
text.formatted: To assess generalization, we also use ManConCorpus <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alamri and Stevenson 2016)</ref>, a manually curated benchmark of contradictory claims from cardiovascular RCT abstracts.

text.text: The two datasets share no abstracts, so ManConCorpus serves as an independent test of DrugCon method generalization.
ManConCorpus is originally structured as question-claim pairs, where each claim, extracted from RCT abstracts, either supports ("yes") or refutes ("no") a clinical question.

To align this setting with our abstract-level contradiction detection task, and to better reflect real-world scenarios where claim annotations are not available for scientific abstracts, we convert the dataset into abstract-to-abstract pairs: two abstracts are labeled as non-contradictory if the pair of associated claims both support the same clinical question or both refute it, and contradictory otherwise.
We construct a question-based split, with 11 questions for training, 6 for development, and 8 for testing.

This design ensures that all abstracts associated with a given clinical question are assigned to a single partition, preventing information leakage across splits and evaluating models' generalization to unseen clinical topics at test time.
All baseline models and the DrugCon framework are evaluated on the test set.

We compare DrugCon's performance with the existing contradiction detection works: (1) a SemRep-based baseline, which we refer to as SemRep-based method, that detects contradictions by identifying pairs of subject-predicate-object triples sharing the same subject and object but exhibiting opposing predicates (e.g., treats vs. causes) (Rosemblat et al. 2019) ; (2) DeBERTa-Base-Con, a sentence-level classification model pretrained on the training part of ManConCorpus dataset (Alamri and Stevenson 2016) with DeBERTa-Base as the backbone model (Makhervaks et al. 2023) for sentence-level contradiction detection; (3) MNLI-MedNLIfoot_0 , a natural language inference (NLI)-based model trained on MNLI (Williams et al. 2018) and MedNLI (Romanov and Shivade 2018), where contradiction detection is formulated as an entailment classification task (Deka et al. 2023).
text.formatted: We compare DrugCon's performance with the existing contradiction detection works: (1) a SemRep-based baseline, which we refer to as SemRep-based method, that detects contradictions by identifying pairs of subject-predicate-object triples sharing the same subject and object but exhibiting opposing predicates (e.g., treats vs. causes) <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Rosemblat et al. 2019)</ref> ; (2) DeBERTa-Base-Con, a sentence-level classification model pretrained on the training part of ManConCorpus dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alamri and Stevenson 2016)</ref> with DeBERTa-Base as the backbone model <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Makhervaks et al. 2023</ref>) for sentence-level contradiction detection; (3) MNLI-MedNLI<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> , a natural language inference (NLI)-based model trained on MNLI <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Williams et al. 2018)</ref> and MedNLI <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Romanov and Shivade 2018)</ref>, where contradiction detection is formulated as an entailment classification task <ref type="bibr">(Deka et al. 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The baseline models operate at the sentence-pair level, whereas our task is end-toend contradiction detection from raw documents, including claim extraction, pairing, and contradiction classification.

For a controlled comparison, we apply all baseline models to the candidate claim pairs generated in the second step of the DrugCon framework (Section 2.2), thereby holding the upstream steps fixed and isolating the contradiction classification component.
Note that none of the baselines produces explanations.
Contradiction explanation is therefore evaluated for DrugCon only.
For contradiction detection, we report precision, recall, and F 1 for the contradictory class.
For contradiction explanation, we report precision, recall, and F 1 for each studylevel factor, and micro-F 1 across all factors.
Explanation is evaluated on the 542 gold contradictory pairs in DrugCon-Bench.
Since the outputs of LLMs vary with the decoding temperature, we evaluate DrugCon under multiple decoding settings to ensure that its performance does not depend on a specific temperature.
Specifically, we run DrugCon at temperatures 0, 0.5, and 1.0, and report the mean and standard deviation over the three runs.
Similarly, we fine-tune DeBERTa-Base-Con with three random seeds and report the mean and standard deviation.

In contrast, the SemRep-based method and MNLI-MedNLI are deterministic, as the SemRep-based method applies fixed rules over SemRep predications and MNLI-MedNLI performs inference with a fixed pretrained checkpoint, so neither involves any random component.
We therefore run each of them once.
The DrugCon framework relies on two prompt-driven LLM components: contradiction detection (Section 2.3) and taxonomy-based contradiction explanation (Section 2.4).
To understand the importance of backbone LLM selection and prompt design, we conduct an ablation study.
We evaluate eleven backbone LLMs.

Seven are open-weight models with known parameter counts, grouped into three size tiers: ≤7B small models (Ministral-3B, Gemma-3-4B), 7-20B medium models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-3-12B), and >20B large models (Gemma-3-27B, Qwen3-32B, Llama-3.3-70B).
text.formatted: Seven are open-weight models with known parameter counts, grouped into three size tiers: ≤7B small models (Ministral-3B, Gemma-3-4B), 7-20B medium models (Llama-3.1-8B, Gemma-3-12B), and >20B large models (Gemma-3-27B, Qwen3-32B, Llama-3.3-70B).

text.text: The remaining four are proprietary models of undisclosed size: Claude-Haiku-4.5, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, GPT-5.5, and GPT-4.1-nano (the backbone used in our main experiments).

For contradiction detection, to assess whether counterfactual reasoning helps uniformly regardless of the backbone model, we compare the counterfactual (CF) prompt, which asks whether one claim could still hold if the other is assumed true (Appendix B.1), against the direct comparison (DC) prompt, which skips the counterfactual reasoning and directly asks whether the two claims draw opposing conclusions about the drug's effect on the disease (Appendix B.2).
For explanation, we use the explanation prompt (Appendix B.3).
All ablations use DrugCon-Bench at temperature 0, holding the upstream claim-extraction and claim-pairing stages fixed so that only the detection and explanation components vary.
We collect 224,756 RCT abstracts published from 2016 to 2025; claim pairing yields 609,877 candidate claim pairs.
As presented in Figure 4, DrugCon identified 615 candidate contradictory pairs from 819 abstracts, and annotators confirmed 494 of them.
text.formatted: As presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>, DrugCon identified 615 candidate contradictory pairs from 819 abstracts, and annotators confirmed 494 of them.

text.text: The exhaustive review found 48 more contradictory pairs.
DrugCon-Bench therefore contains 542 (494+48) contradictory claim pairs from 819 abstracts.
Interannotator agreement (Gwet's AC1) in the final round was 0.812-0.839 (mean 0.821) for contradiction identification and 0.645-0.725 (mean 0.679) for factor labeling.
A contradiction can be explained by more than one contextual factor.
In DrugCon-Bench, 75.5% of the contradictory pairs are annotated with two or more factors (2.18 factors per pair on average), so the percentages of factor distribution sum to more than 100%.

The most common factors are Outcome measures (64.0%), Population (51.3%), and Dosage and exposure duration (35.6%), followed by Study design (20.3%), Combined drug effects (10.0%), and Route of administration (9.0%)(Figure 5).

text.text: DrugCon significantly outperforms all baselines, with a precision of 0.636, recall of 0.896, and F 1 score of 0.744.

In contrast, all baseline methods exhibit lower performance: • The rule-based SemRep-based method detects only 4 contradictions (2 correct), yielding a precision of 0.5 and extremely low recall (2/542).

As discussed in its original work (Rosemblat et al. 2019), it captures apparent contradictions based on surface-level subject-predicate-object patterns, but fails to identify contextdependent or implicit contradictions, which are prevalent in DrugCon-Bench.
text.formatted: As discussed in its original work <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Rosemblat et al. 2019)</ref>, it captures apparent contradictions based on surface-level subject-predicate-object patterns, but fails to identify contextdependent or implicit contradictions, which are prevalent in DrugCon-Bench.

text.text: • The domain-specific model DeBERTa-Base-Con, trained on cardiology sentence pairs from ManConCorpus, does not generalize to DrugCon-Bench (F1 =0.000), due to its cardiology focus.
• The NLI model, MNLI-MedNLI, identifies a small number of contradictions (recall: 0.106) but with very low precision (0.017).
Despite being trained on the NLI corpus that covers general biomedical domain, it shows a tendency toward predicting "contradiction" for non-contradictory pairs in DrugCon-Bench.
Table 2 also reports contradiction detection performance on the ManConCorpus test set.

The relative ordering of methods is consistent with our findings on DrugCon-Bench: DrugCon again achieves the best performance (F 1 0.502), significantly outperforming DeBERTa-Base-Con (0.333) and MNLI-MedNLI (0.168), with SemRep-based method again failing to detect any contradictions.
The main difference is that DrugCon scores lower on ManConCorpus than on DrugCon-Bench (F 1 0.502 vs.
0.744), driven by lower recall (0.380 vs.
0.896), whereas DeBERTa-Base-Con and MNLI-MedNLI achieve higher recall on ManConCorpus (0.269 and 0.292) than on DrugCon-Bench (0.000 and 0.106).
We further evaluate how well DrugCon identifies the study-level factors that explain contradictions using our proposed taxonomy.
Results are shown in Figure 5 (right).

text.text: DrugCon attains an overall micro F 1 of 0.482, where performance varies across factors.
It performs best on the frequently occurring factors that are typically stated explicitly in RCT abstracts, including Outcome measures (F1 =0.659), Population (F1 =0.
573), and Dosage/exposure duration (F1 =0.517), indicating that the framework performs best on the dominant sources of disagreement.
The moderate overall score reflects lower performance on rarer and more implicit factors, which we analyze below.

0.649; OpenAI's smallest and lowest-cost GPT-4.1 variant), as does Gemma-3-27B (0.678 vs.
Under the direct comparison prompt, these smaller models over-predict contradictions, achieving very high recall but low precision (e.g., Gemma-3-12B reaches 0.996 recall at 0.378 precision).

Larger models are substantially more expensive: at the scale of 224,756 abstracts and 609,877 candidate pairs, running detection with GPT-5.5 or Claude-Sonnet-4.5 would cost approximately $5,500 and $2,800, respectively, compared with approximately $80 for GPT-4.1-nano.

We presented DrugCon, an LLM-based framework for large-scale detection and structured explanation of contradictory drug-disease associations in RCT literature.
Across both DrugCon-Bench and the external ManConCorpus benchmark, DrugCon with the GPT-4.1-nano backbone outperformed rule-based, supervised, and NLIbased baselines for contradiction detection.

Beyond detection, DrugCon provides structured explanations based on study-level factors: it is effective at identifying differences in frequently occurring and explicit study factors, such as outcome measures, population, and dosage, but struggles with more implicit factors, such as evolving scientific evidence and ambiguous referents.
These findings suggest that LLM-based reasoning is effective for large-scale contradiction analysis, while challenges remain in reasoning over scientific context and resolving implicit study factors.

Existing approaches rely on lexical opposition and sentence-level information (Kim et al. 2006; Alamri 2016; Tawfik and Spruit 2018; Yazi et al. 2021; Makhervaks et al. 2023), which fail to capture implicit or cross-sentence knowledge.
text.formatted: Existing approaches rely on lexical opposition and sentence-level information <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Kim et al. 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Alamri 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Tawfik and Spruit 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Yazi et al. 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Makhervaks et al. 2023)</ref>, which fail to capture implicit or cross-sentence knowledge.

text.text: Our results suggest that contradiction detection in DrugCon-Bench instead requires implicit reasoning over the scientific claims.
Many contradictory pairs do not contain explicit opposing statements (e.g., "effective" versus "ineffective"), but instead express disagreement through conditional statements or indirect assertions.
Determining whether two claims are contradictory therefore requires interpreting the meaning and scope of the claims rather than relying on surface lexical cues or predicate oppositions.
DrugCon addresses this by using an LLM to reason over the semantic implications of scientific claims and to integrate contextual information across multiple sentences.
The following contradictory pair, which DrugCon identified but the baseline models missed, illustrates a contradiction that requires reasoning beyond explicit opposing statements:
Claim 1: "Exercise was effective in reducing fall-related injuries among communitydwelling older women at a moderate cost.
Vitamin D supplementation had marginal additional benefit."

(PMID 26205890) Claim 2: "Our data suggest that vitamin D supplementation positively affected the rehabilitation program in patients [. . . ] by reducing the risk of falls and improving postural stability."
The contradiction appears only when the two sentences of Claim 1 are read together: the "additional benefit" of vitamin D refers to the fall-related injuries mentioned in the previous sentence.
Claim 1 thus indicates that vitamin D adds little to fall prevention, whereas Claim 2 reports that it reduces the risk of falls.
Detecting this conflict requires cross-sentence reasoning and interpreting "marginal additional benefit" as a negative finding, rather than matching opposing words.

The lower recall of DrugCon on ManConCorpus can be mainly attributed to the definition of contradiction in ManConCorpus: each clinical question is paired with several claims that answer "Yes" or "No" to it, rather than with claims aligned on a specific relation.
The following sample illustrates this:
Question: "In patients with coronary artery disease, is mutation or polymorphisms in endothelial nitric oxide synthase gene associated with CAD or MI or ACS development?"

Claim 1: "We conclude that the E/D298 polymorphism is most consistently associated with CAD, but not with progression of atherosclerosis" (PMID 15068395, labeled "yes") Claim 2: "These findings suggest that the 894G>T, -786T>C and 4a/4b polymorphisms of the NOS3 were not associated with CAD in the studied subjects." (PMID 19931521, labeled "no") Because the two claims answer the question differently ("yes" vs. "no"), this pair is labeled as contradictory under our conversion of ManConCorpus (Section 2.6.1), while DrugCon labels it as non-contradictory.
text.formatted: Claim 1: "We conclude that the E/D298 polymorphism is most consistently associated with CAD, but not with progression of atherosclerosis" (PMID 15068395, labeled "yes") Claim 2: "These findings suggest that the 894G>T, -786T>C and 4a/4b polymorphisms of the NOS3 were not associated with CAD in the studied subjects." <ref type="bibr">(PMID 19931521, labeled "no")</ref> Because the two claims answer the question differently ("yes" vs. "no"), this pair is labeled as contradictory under our conversion of ManConCorpus (Section 2.6.1), while DrugCon labels it as non-contradictory.

text.text: The two claims appear to examine different polymorphisms of the same gene (NOS3).
Therefore, whether they are contradictory depends on the level of comparison.
The claims may be contradictory at the gene level but compatible at the level of polymorphism each study examines.
This ambiguity arises because ManConCorpus links claims through a shared high-level question rather than an explicitly aligned relation.
This comparison highlights another important contribution of this work: the construction of DrugCon-Bench.
DrugCon-Bench reduces the ambiguity above by grounding each pair in an aligned drug-disease association and annotating contradictions directly at the claim level.

It also provides a closed evaluation environment in which all pairwise contradictions within a subset of abstracts are exhaustively annotated, addressing a key limitation of the prior dataset (Alamri and Stevenson 2016), which provides only partial annotations of contradictory evidence.
text.formatted: It also provides a closed evaluation environment in which all pairwise contradictions within a subset of abstracts are exhaustively annotated, addressing a key limitation of the prior dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alamri and Stevenson 2016)</ref>, which provides only partial annotations of contradictory evidence.

text.text: These properties support more precise and rigorous evaluation of contradiction detection systems in biomedical text.
A key contribution of this work is the extension from contradiction detection to contradiction explanation by study-level differences.
Existing studies operate at the sentence level and treat contradiction detection as a binary task (Kim et al. 2006; Alamri 2016; Tawfik and Spruit 2018; Yazi et al. 2021; Makhervaks et al. 2023).
text.formatted: Existing studies operate at the sentence level and treat contradiction detection as a binary task <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Kim et al. 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Alamri 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Tawfik and Spruit 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Yazi et al. 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Makhervaks et al. 2023)</ref>.

text.text: DrugCon not only enables multi-sentence reasoning using LLMs, but also extends contradiction detection to structured explanation: it leverages the full abstract context to identify differences in study-level factors between two contradictory claims, such as population, dosage, and outcome measures, which may explain their different findings.
DrugCon performs best on the factors that are stated explicitly in RCT abstracts, including Outcome measures (F1 =0.659), Population (F1 =0.573), and Dosage/exposure duration (F1 =0.517).

However, DrugCon shows lower performance on the following relatively implicit factors: • Evolving scientific evidence (F1=0.103) is annotated when conflicting claims reflect different stages of scientific understanding.

As illustrated by the eplerenone-heart failure pair in Table 1, the earlier study (PMID 33175088) reports an inconclusive finding due to inadequate statistical power, while the later study (PMID 37370197) reports significant clinical benefits.
text.formatted: As illustrated by the eplerenone-heart failure pair in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>, the earlier study (PMID 33175088) reports an inconclusive finding due to inadequate statistical power, while the later study (PMID 37370197) reports significant clinical benefits.

text.text: Identifying this factor requires recognizing different time points of two studies.
However, the current prompt design directs the model to focus solely on the abstract, which limits its ability to perform such temporal reasoning.

Determining how two articles relate to one another, for example whether a later trial was designed to confirm, extend, or overturn an earlier one, requires information beyond the abstract, such as publication dates, citation links, shared trial registrations, and funding sources.
Modeling such inter-article relationships needs further exploration in the future works.
• Combined drug effects (F1=0.000) is annotated for difference in co-administrations.
As illustrated by the candesartan-left ventricular function pair in Table 1, candesartan is evaluated in combination with anthracycline in one study and trastuzumab in another.
text.formatted: As illustrated by the candesartan-left ventricular function pair in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>, candesartan is evaluated in combination with anthracycline in one study and trastuzumab in another.

text.text: However, the LLM's output for this pair labels the contradiction as Study design, explaining that the two studies differ in their trial designs.
Although the LLM generated reasoning acknowledges the difference in co-administered drugs, the LLM attributes the difference to broader study design difference rather than to Combined drug effects.
This suggests DrugCon's low performance on Combined drug effects stems from the model attributing the co-administration situation to a more general category.
• For Known controversy (F1=0.000), DrugCon fails to identify any cases.

This factor is annotated based on lexical cues, such as direct acknowledgment of further analysis requirement, uncertainty, or inconclusiveness within a claim, rather than differences between studies.
As illustrated by the melatonin-preoperative anxiety pair in Table 1, Study 2 (PMID 37953202) explicitly acknowledges that early termination of the trial increases the likelihood of bias.
text.formatted: As illustrated by the melatonin-preoperative anxiety pair in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>, Study 2 (PMID 37953202) explicitly acknowledges that early termination of the trial increases the likelihood of bias.

text.text: However, the LLM's generated reasoning over the contexts of this pair does not identify the self-acknowledged uncertainty of the claim 2.

This suggests the prompt, currently designed to compare study factor differences between the study contexts described in the two abstracts, requires a further reasoning step for checking uncertainty markers within a single claim first.
• For Ambiguous referent, which is annotated when one claim lacks explicit contextual information such as dosage or population, DrugCon fails to identify any cases (F1=0.000).
This failure stems from the prompt design rather than a fundamental limitation of LLMs.

The current prompt instructs the model to assign the studylevel factors that explain the contradiction based on differences between the two abstracts, so it is never asked to assess whether a factor is absent from an abstract.

This suggests that explanation should be reframed as explicit extraction of each study-level factor, where "not reported" is a valid value, so that missing contextual information is identified directly rather than inferred.
Such a structured extraction step could be further supported by checking the reporting completeness of each factor against established checklist items (Jiang et al. 2024 (Jiang et al. , 2025)).
text.formatted: Such a structured extraction step could be further supported by checking the reporting completeness of each factor against established checklist items <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Jiang et al. 2024</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Jiang et al. , 2025))</ref>.

text.text: Stronger backbones improve overall explanation performance (micro-F 1 up to 0.603 for GPT-5.5; Table 3), but the implicit, low-support factors remain the hardest: even the best backbone attains only F1 =0.436 on evolving scientific evidence and 0.022 on ambiguous referents.
text.formatted: Stronger backbones improve overall explanation performance (micro-F 1 up to 0.603 for GPT-5.5; Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">3</ref>), but the implicit, low-support factors remain the hardest: even the best backbone attains only F1 =0.436 on evolving scientific evidence and 0.022 on ambiguous referents.

text.text: This is consistent with the error analysis above, as these failures arise from missing information and prompt design rather than from model capability alone.
The ablation results (Section 3.4) show that no single prompt is best for every backbone, so prompt design and model choice should be considered together.

Under the direct comparison prompt, smaller models over-predict contradictions, likely because judging whether two claims contradict in a single step provides little structure to guide a weaker model's reasoning.

The counterfactual prompt mitigates this problem by requiring an explicit, step-by-step check of whether the two claims can co-exist, which reduces over-prediction and improves precision (Wei et al. 2022).
text.formatted: The counterfactual prompt mitigates this problem by requiring an explicit, step-by-step check of whether the two claims can co-exist, which reduces over-prediction and improves precision <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Wei et al. 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Larger models, in contrast, can more reliably judge whether two claims contradict in a single step, so the explicit reasoning steps of the counterfactual prompt provide little additional benefit.
These stronger backbones, however, would cost roughly 35-70 times more than GPT-4.1-nano at the scale of this study.

For explanation, performance increases with model capability, suggesting that identifying study-level factors, particularly the rarer and more implicit ones, requires deeper reasoning over the full abstract context.
Contradictory claims across RCTs present a challenge for evidence-based medicine (Prasad et al. 2013).
text.formatted: Contradictory claims across RCTs present a challenge for evidence-based medicine <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Prasad et al. 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Medical practitioners, clinicians, and clinical guideline developers should be careful when retrieving scientific findings to support their decisions.
Ideally, all relevant findings, including contradictory results, should be considered to inform a more complete understanding of the evidence.
DrugCon provides a scalable mechanism for identifying contradictory evidence and surfacing study-level factors that may explain these disagreements.

In clinical decision-making, by explicitly highlighting differences in populations, drug administration, or outcome definitions, DrugCon surfaces structured context that clinicians would otherwise need to identify manually across multiple studies.

As discussed in the sample for Population in Table 1, when two studies report contradictory findings on effectiveness of indomethacin to treat post-ERCP pancreatitis, DrugCon highlights that the studies were conducted in different patient populations.
text.formatted: As discussed in the sample for Population in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>, when two studies report contradictory findings on effectiveness of indomethacin to treat post-ERCP pancreatitis, DrugCon highlights that the studies were conducted in different patient populations.

text.text: This enables clinicians to assess which evidence is more applicable to their specific patient group.
By making such study-level differences explicit, DrugCon could support more informed and nuanced interpretation of clinical findings.
DrugCon supports evidence synthesis by explicitly identifying the contradictory findings and the study-level differences underlying the contradictions.
Firstly, contradictions across biomedical publications can hinder understanding of the current state of evidence, which challenges evidence review.

The automated identification of contradictory claims therefore is important to support systematic reviewers and literature surveillance systems by highlighting findings that require closer examination (Ioannidis 2016; Kilicoglu 2018).

Additionally, the identified study-level differences support the meta-analyses to capture the study-level variations when aggregating the results of multiple independent studies that address the same research question (Choi and Kang 2025).
For knowledge graph construction, DrugCon can support the development of more context-aware representations of biomedical knowledge.

Existing biomedical knowledge graphs often aggregate findings from multiple publications into unified subject-predicate-object relations (Kilicoglu et al. 2012), where contradictory findings may coexist without explicit contextual information.
text.formatted: Existing biomedical knowledge graphs often aggregate findings from multiple publications into unified subject-predicate-object relations <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Kilicoglu et al. 2012)</ref>, where contradictory findings may coexist without explicit contextual information.

text.text: When two contradictory claims coexist in the knowledge graph, it is not always clear which claim should be trusted (Sosa and Altman 2022).
text.formatted: When two contradictory claims coexist in the knowledge graph, it is not always clear which claim should be trusted <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Sosa and Altman 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Current approaches to managing such contradictions rely on confidence scoring by source weighting (Wang et al. 2023), which may result in information loss by collapsing multiple context and metadata into a single score.
text.formatted: Current approaches to managing such contradictions rely on confidence scoring by source weighting <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Wang et al. 2023)</ref>, which may result in information loss by collapsing multiple context and metadata into a single score.

text.text: The alternative approach could be representing claims together with their contextual characteristics, such as patient populations, outcome measures, and study design (Rosemblat et al. 2019).
text.formatted: The alternative approach could be representing claims together with their contextual characteristics, such as patient populations, outcome measures, and study design <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Rosemblat et al. 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Rather than resolving contradictions by discarding or down-weighting claims, this preserves the full evidential context.
By linking claims to their study-level factors, DrugCon preserves contextual information with the knowledge.

This supports the construction of publication-specific or claim-centered knowledge graphs, enabling users to assess not only whether a relationship has been reported, but also under what conditions it was observed and whether contradictory evidence exists.
The large-scale contradiction analysis by DrugCon is also important for biomedical knowledge processing.

Over 40 millions biomedical publications has been indexed in PubMed (Jin et al. 2024), which makes it practically impossible for clinicians and researchers to manually track the contradictory evidence across literature.
text.formatted: Over 40 millions biomedical publications has been indexed in PubMed <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Jin et al. 2024)</ref>, which makes it practically impossible for clinicians and researchers to manually track the contradictory evidence across literature.

text.text: DrugCon provides the scalable solution to processing this large-scale publications to support the downstream application of knowledge synthesis for clinicians, systematic reviewers, and knowledge graph developers.
Our study has several limitations.
First, DrugCon is evaluated on RCT abstracts only.
Although abstracts typically summarize the key findings and study characteristics (Schulz et al. 2010), they might omit details that might be relevant for explaining contradictory findings.
text.formatted: Although abstracts typically summarize the key findings and study characteristics <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Schulz et al. 2010)</ref>, they might omit details that might be relevant for explaining contradictory findings.

text.text: Second, the DrugCon pipeline achieved an overall F1 score of 0.482 on the study-level factor difference identification.

While the framework effectively identifies frequent factors such as outcome measures and population differences, it fails to identify combined drug effects, known controversy, and ambiguous referents, and rarely identifies evolving scientific evidence.
Third, our contradiction taxonomy, adapted and extended from the previous work (Rosemblat et al. 2019), focuses on ten study-level factors.
text.formatted: Third, our contradiction taxonomy, adapted and extended from the previous work <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Rosemblat et al. 2019)</ref>, focuses on ten study-level factors.

text.text: Although these factors capture many common sources of disagreement, they may not fully represent all reasons underlying contradictory findings.

Applying DrugCon to 224,756 RCT abstracts, we constructed DrugCon-Bench, a benchmark of exhaustively annotated contradictory claim pairs that supports closed-world evaluation of both contradiction detection and explanation.

Across DrugCon-Bench and the external ManConCorpus benchmark, DrugCon outperforms rule-based, supervised, and NLI-based baselines, and moves beyond detection to identify the study-level factors that may explain why studies disagree.
These results show that LLM-based reasoning is effective for large-scale contradiction analysis, while interpreting more implicit sources of disagreement remains challenging.

In future work, we will incorporate inter-article information (e.g., publication dates, citation links, and trial registrations) and reframe explanation as explicit extraction of each study-level factor (Section 4.2).

We also plan to leverage the links between claims and their study-level factors to construct claim-centered knowledge graphs and evidence synthesis tools, enabling users to assess not only whether a drug-disease association has been reported, but also under what conditions it was observed and whether contradictory evidence exists.

Evolving scientific evidence.
Contradictions due to updated scientific understanding or revised hypotheses.

Task: Decide whether two biomedical claims about the same drug-disease association present a contradiction, using counterfactual reasoning.
(1) Assume Claim 1 is true.
Under this assumption, would Claim 2's overall assessment of the drug for the disease still hold?
(2) Assume Claim 2 is true.
Under this assumption, would Claim 1's overall assessment of the drug for the disease still hold?

Definition: A "contradiction" here is an apparent contradiction: the two claims give opposing overall assessments of the same drug for the same disease (e.g., effective vs. ineffective, beneficial vs. harmful, safe vs. unsafe).
It need not be a strict logical impossibility.

Task Notes: (a) The two claims are contradictory if either (1) or (2) reveals that the overall assessments oppose each other. (b) A contradiction may be partial: if one subclaim or subpoint in a claim opposes the other claim, treat the pair as contradictory, even if other parts agree. (c) Do not dismiss a contradiction merely because the two studies differ in outcome measured, patient subgroup, dose, duration, timing, comparator, or study design.

Opposing conclusions still count as a contradiction even if they could be reconciled by such differences. (d) Classify as "Claims can coexist" only if the claims concern different drugs or diseases, express the same overall direction, or make no clear assessment of the drug-disease association.

text.text: Task: Determine whether two biomedical claims contain a potential contradiction about the same drug-disease association.
For this task, "contradiction" means a potential contradiction in the overall assessment of the drug for the disease, not a strict logical impossibility.

Focus only on: • the drug, treatment, or intervention • the disease, condition, or indication • the overall direction/valence of the claim about that drug-disease association Classify as "Contradiction exists" if the claims concern the same drug or drug class and the same disease/condition, and their overall assessments are discordant.
Do not reject a contradiction merely because the claims differ in population, outcome, endpoint, biomarker, comparator, dose, duration, study design, or statistical method.
Classify as "Claims can coexist" only if the claims are about different drugs or diseases, share the same overall direction, or do not make a clear assessment of the drug-disease association.
Task Notes: Keep the reasoning short and direct.
Identify the drug, the disease, and the overall direction of each claim.

text.text: Task: Given two biomedical claims that appear to report opposing outcomes for the same drug-disease association, analyze whether the apparent contradiction can be explained by differences in study-level contextual conditions.
Specifically: (1) Examine Claim 1 together with its source abstract.
(2) Examine Claim 2 together with its source abstract.

(3) Determine whether the opposing outcomes can be explained by one or more contextual factors from the taxonomy below, and provide an appropriate explanation of how each identified factor accounts for the contradiction.
Internal-to-patient factors: • Species.
The claims are based on different species, where differences in disease manifestation, biological mechanisms, and pharmacokinetics across species limit the direct comparability of drug effects.
• Population.
The claims target different human subpopulations (e.g., age, sex, genetics, comorbidities, ethnicity, or risk profiles).
External-to-patient factors: • Dosage and exposure duration.
The same intervention is administered at different doses or exposure durations, which may produce different biological effects.
• Route or mode of administration.
The intervention is delivered via different routes or timing, which may change tissue targeting or absorption.
• Evolving scientific evidence.
The claims reflect different stages of scientific understanding, where early hypotheses are later revised by subsequent work.
• Known controversy.
One or both claims explicitly acknowledge uncertainty, debate, or conditional validity, indicating an ongoing scientific controversy rather than a definitive conclusion.
• Combined drug effect.
The reported effect of a drug depends on its combination with other medications, where drug-drug interactions or synergistic effects produce outcomes that differ across studies.
• Study design.
The studies differ in trial methodology, such as parallel vs.
crossover design, superiority vs. non-inferiority frameworks, blinding status, comparator type (placebo vs. active control), or randomization procedures.
• Outcome measures.
The studies assess different outcomes or evaluate the same outcome at different time points.
• Ambiguous referent.
One claim lacks a clear specification of species, population, dosage and exposure duration, or route of administration, resulting in uncertainty about the basis of comparison.
Task Notes: Base your analysis strictly on the provided claims and abstracts.
Do not use external biomedical knowledge.
Do not speculate beyond what is explicitly stated in the text.

Introduction.
Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold standard of biomedical evidence, while their findings can sometimes be contradictory.
Drug-disease associations are especially important because they directly guide clinical decisions, inform drug repurposing efforts, and support health policy.
Contradictory findings across studies can create confusion, hinder reliable evidence synthesis, and slow down the translation of research into practice.

It is important to develop automated systems that can systematically detect and resolve contradictory drug-disease claims, providing clinicians and researchers with a clearer, more reliable evidence base.
To address this, we developed an LLM-based framework to identify potential contradictions across large-scale RCT articles.
The framework consists of: • Claim Extraction: extracting scientific claims from RCT abstracts.
• Related Claim Pairing: pairing semantically related claims using rule-based methods and dense embeddings.
• Contradiction Detection: using LLM prompting to determine whether claim pairs are contradictory.
